newsitem.title: USA: Clinton said set for Paula Jones court fight.
newsitem.headline: Clinton said set for Paula Jones court fight.

text.p: President Bill Clinton will defend himself in court rather than apologise in the sexual harassment case that Paula Jones, a former Arkansas state employee, has brought against him, Clinton's personal lawyer said on Sunday.

But the lawyer, Robert Bennett, said he was ready to recommend that Clinton make a charitable donation and help defray Jones' legal costs as part of an out-of-court settlement that would involve paying no more than $700,000.
"No apology, no admission of misconduct and we're not going to line her pockets or her lawyers' pockets," Bennett said in summing up the president's position about any future settlement.

"We're the laughingstock of the world when we allow this kind of nonsense to go on," he added on the NBC programme "Meet the Press." He said the case was about Jones' trying to drag Clinton into the gutter and cash in on book and movie deals.
Jones' lawyers, Joseph Cammarata and Gilbert Davis, in separately aired interviews, said in the absence of an apology from Clinton, their client would demand her day in court.
"The core feature of a settlement is not money. Ten million dollars wouldn't do this. It's going to have to redeem her reputation," Davis said on the ABC programme "This Week."
"What they're trying to do is buy her off so she'll walk away and not be worried about her reputation," Davis added.

Initially, Jones sought $700,000 in damages for an unwanted sexual overture she maintains Clinton, then the governor of Arkansas, made to her in a Little Rock hotel room in 1991, when she was a state employee.

Her suit, filed in 1994, claims that Clinton used the powers of the governor's office to violate her civil rights. Last week, the Supreme Court rejected Clinton's appeal for a delay in proceedings in the suit until after he leaves the White House.
The 9-0 court ruling set the stage for a new round of discussions about a possible out-of-court settlement.
But Bennett, throwing down a gauntlet, said: the President of the United States will not apologise to Paula Jones. He will not apologise for something that he never did."
Nor would Clinton "admit to conduct which did not occur for the sake of getting this behind him," the lawyer said. He added that he had consulted the president on Saturday night.
Bennett said he would recommend against any settlement clause that would let people "conclude that the financial terms were such was that he must have done what was alleged in the complaint."

"If she insists on a trial, we'll have a trial," Bennett told ABC News. "I notice a certain amount of cockiness out there, and as my mother once said to me, be careful what you wish for, you might get it."
He added: "So if they're insisting on proceeding, we'll proceed."
Jones alleged that Clinton made sexual advances to her in a Little Rock hotel room on May 8, 1991, including exposing himself to her and asking her to perform oral sex.

She contends that she took the legal action to clear her name after American Spectator published an article claiming that Arkansas state policemen set up sexual liaisons for Clinton. One of the women in the article was identified by the name "Paula." Jones alleged this tied her to the case.
Clinton denies the allegations. The Supreme Court made no ruling on the merits of Jones' case, but said a sitting president can be sued for actions outside the scope of his official duties.
"This is an attempt to humiliate the president," Bennett said on CNN. He said he would file a motion for dismissal of the case.
